questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a public sector bank in India as of August 2020?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kotak Mahindra Bank**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Public Sector Banks (PSBs):** These are banks in which the government of India holds a majority stake (more than 50%). They are owned and operated by the government. Examples include **Canara Bank, Punjab National Bank (PNB), and Indian Bank**.
 
• **Canara Bank:** It is one of the largest public sector banks in India, established in **1906**. It became a PSB after its nationalization in **1969**. *Hence, it is a public sector bank.*
 
• **Punjab National Bank (PNB):** Established in **1894**, it is another leading public sector bank in India. After the nationalization in 1969, it became a government-owned entity. *Hence, it is a public sector bank.*
 
• **Indian Bank:** It was established in **1907** and nationalized in **1969**. It is a public sector bank with the government holding a majority stake. *Hence, it is a public sector bank.*
 
• **Kotak Mahindra Bank:** It is a private sector bank, established in **2003**. It is not owned by the government and operates as a private financial institution. *Hence, it is NOT a public sector bank.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Kotak Mahindra Bank.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Public Sector Banks in India:**

 
 
• Public sector banks are a crucial part of India's banking system, contributing significantly to **financial inclusion** and economic development.
 
• Examples of PSBs include **State Bank of India (SBI), Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, and Canara Bank**.
 
• These banks are known for their wide network of branches, government support, and focus on providing services to rural and underserved areas.
 
 
 
• **Private Sector Banks:**
 
 
• Private sector banks are owned by private entities or corporations, and their operations are driven by profits and market competition.
 
• Examples include **HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, and Kotak Mahindra Bank**.
 
• They focus on providing modern banking services, technological advancements, and customized financial products.
 
 
 
• **Key Differences:**
 
 
• **Ownership:** PSBs are owned by the government, while private banks are owned by private entities.
 
• **Focus:** PSBs prioritize social objectives like financial inclusion, whereas private banks emphasize profitability and customer-centric services.
 
• **Examples:** Canara Bank is a PSB, while Kotak Mahindra Bank is a private bank.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Kotak Mahindra Bank:**

 
 
• **Founded:** It was established in **2003** and is headquartered in **Mumbai, Maharashtra**.
 
• **Services:** It provides a range of financial services such as **loans, deposits, credit cards, investment solutions, and insurance products**.
 
 
 
• **Nationalization of Banks:**
 
 
• **1969:** The government nationalized 14 major private sector banks, including PNB and Canara Bank, to strengthen the economy and ensure equitable distribution of credit.
 
• **1980:** Another six banks were nationalized, expanding the reach of PSBs to rural and underserved areas.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a Shaiva cult?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pancharatra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Shaiva cult** refers to religious sects and traditions that worship **Lord Shiva** as the supreme deity.
 
• **Veerashaiva**, **Pashupatha**, and **Kapalika** are prominent sects associated with Shaivism. These sects have distinct philosophies and practices centered around **Lord Shiva**. *Hence, these are Shaiva cults.*
 
• **Pancharatra** is a sect associated with **Vaishnavism**, where followers worship **Lord Vishnu** as the supreme deity. It is not related to Shaivism. *Hence, this is NOT a Shaiva cult.*
 
• **Kapalika** is a Shaiva sect known for its extreme and esoteric practices. It emphasizes asceticism and the worship of Shiva in fierce forms like Bhairava. *Hence, this is a Shaiva cult.*
 
• **Pashupatha** is one of the oldest Shaiva sects, focusing on devotion to Lord Shiva and the renunciation of worldly attachments. It was founded by **Lakulisha**. *Hence, this is a Shaiva cult.*
 
• **Veerashaiva** is a Shaiva tradition rooted in devotion to Lord Shiva. It originated in South India and emphasizes equality and devotion. *Hence, this is a Shaiva cult.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Pancharatra.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pancharatra:**

 
 
• **Origin:** Pancharatra is a sect of **Vaishnavism**, which worships **Lord Vishnu** and his incarnations.
 
• **Philosophy:** It focuses on the worship of Vishnu and his manifestations in five forms: **Para, Vyuhas, Vibhava, Antaryami, and Archavatara**.
 
• **Scriptures:** The sect derives its teachings from texts like **Pancharatra Agamas**.
 
• **Practices:** Rituals include temple worship, chanting, and devotion to Vishnu. It is prominent in South India.
 
 
 
• **Shaiva Cults:**
 
 
• **Veerashaiva:** Originating in South India, it emphasizes **devotion to Shiva** and equality. It was led by **Basavanna**.
 
• **Pashupatha:** One of the oldest Shaiva sects, it focuses on asceticism and devotion. Founded by **Lakulisha**.
 
• **Kapalika:** Known for its esoteric practices, it worships Shiva in fierce forms like **Bhairava**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Shaivism:** A major sect in Hinduism that worships **Lord Shiva**. It has various sub-sects like **Pashupatha** and **Kapalika**.
 
• **Vaishnavism:** A sect in Hinduism that worships **Lord Vishnu**. Pancharatra belongs to this tradition.
 
• **Geographical Influence:** Shaivism is prominent in **South India**, while Vaishnavism also flourishes in the same region.

questions.question: Under the Rules of Lok Sabha, the 'Leader of the House' means the ______, if he is a member of the Lok Sabha.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Prime Minister**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Leader of the House** in the Lok Sabha is the **Prime Minister**, provided he/she is a member of the Lok Sabha. This is according to the **Rules of Lok Sabha**.
 
• The Leader of the House plays a vital role in coordinating legislative activities, addressing the priorities of the government, and representing the government's position in parliamentary debates.
 
• The **Leader of the House** is appointed by the **Prime Minister** or designated by the ruling party. In most cases, it is the Prime Minister themselves who occupies this position. *Hence, the correct answer is Prime Minister.*
 
• Other parliamentary roles such as the **Speaker** and **Deputy Speaker** are responsible for presiding over the proceedings and maintaining order, but they do not act as the Leader of the House.
 
• The **President** does not have a role in the legislative functioning of the Lok Sabha as he/she represents the head of state and not the government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Leader of the House:**

 
 
• The **Leader of the House** is responsible for facilitating the smooth functioning of the House and ensuring the government’s legislative agenda is carried forward.
 
• This position is crucial in resolving conflicts, negotiating with opposition parties, and representing the government’s stance on various issues.
 
 
 
• **Roles of Other Positions:**
 
 
• **Speaker:** The Speaker presides over sessions of the Lok Sabha, ensures the decorum of debates, and decides on procedural matters.
 
• **Deputy Speaker:** The Deputy Speaker assists the Speaker and presides over the House in the Speaker’s absence.
 
• **President:** The President of India is the ceremonial head of state and does not participate in the legislative proceedings of the Lok Sabha.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• The position of Leader of the House has been held by prominent leaders such as **Jawaharlal Nehru**, **Indira Gandhi**, and **Atal Bihari Vajpayee**, showcasing its importance in parliamentary democracy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Prime Minister:**

 
 
• The Prime Minister represents the government in the Lok Sabha and leads all legislative and executive decision-making processes.
 
• This position signifies the leadership of the ruling party and ensures the implementation of government policies.
 
 
 
• **Speaker and Deputy Speaker:**
 
 
• The Speaker and Deputy Speaker are non-partisan positions and focus primarily on the proceedings and functioning of the House.
 
• Their roles are distinct from the Leader of the House, who is actively involved in policymaking and legislative discussions.

questions.question: The powers, privileges and immunities of either House of the Indian Parliament and of its members and committees are laid down in Article ______ of the Constitution of India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 105**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 105** of the **Constitution of India** specifies the **powers, privileges, and immunities** of the members of Parliament and its committees.
 
• It grants **freedom of speech in Parliament** to members, ensuring they can express their views without fear of legal consequences. *Hence, the correct option is Article 105.*
 
• This article also protects members from any proceedings in courts for anything said or done within Parliament, ensuring that parliamentary discussions remain open and free.
 
• The privileges under Article 105 are not absolute. Parliament has the power to codify these privileges, although it has not yet been done comprehensively.
 
• The **immunities** include freedom from arrest in certain civil cases during a session and the privilege of not being summoned to a court of law as witnesses during parliamentary sessions.
 
• **Article 105(3)** states that the powers, privileges, and immunities of Parliament and its members shall be the same as those of the British House of Commons until defined by Indian law.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Article 105.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 105 of the Constitution:**

 
 
• **Freedom of speech:** Members of Parliament are granted freedom of speech within the house, which is a cornerstone of democratic governance.
 
• Parliamentary privileges ensure that **MPs can participate freely** in discussions without outside interference.
 
• These privileges are aimed at maintaining the independence and dignity of the Parliament.
 
 
 
• **Comparison to British House of Commons:**
 
 
• The privileges under **Article 105(3)** are modeled on the British House of Commons, but they have yet to be fully codified in India.
 
• These include immunity from court proceedings for actions taken in Parliament and the ability to regulate its own procedures.
 
 
 
• **Relevant Supreme Court Judgments:**
 
 
• The **Keshav Singh case (1965)** highlighted that parliamentary privileges are subject to constitutional limitations.
 
• In the **PV Narasimha Rao case (1998)**, the Supreme Court ruled that parliamentary immunity extends to actions like accepting bribes if done within the Parliament.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Related Articles:**

 
 
• **Article 194:** Similar to Article 105, it outlines the powers, privileges, and immunities of state legislatures and their members.
 
• **Article 124:** Deals with the establishment and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India.
 
• **Article 302:** Relates to the power of Parliament to impose restrictions on trade, commerce, and intercourse among states.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Parliamentary Privileges:**
 
 
• These privileges are essential for ensuring **free discussions and debates** in Parliament, which is vital for democracy.
 
• They protect members from external influences and pressures, allowing them to perform their duties effectively.

questions.question: 'Harela', the harvesting festival, is celebrated in the state of ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttarakhand**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Harela** is a traditional festival celebrated in the state of **Uttarakhand**, India.
 
• The word **"Harela"** translates to **"Day of Green"** in the local Kumaoni and Garhwali languages of Uttarakhand.
 
• This festival is observed to mark the **onset of the monsoon season** and the beginning of the sowing cycle in agriculture, making it a significant festival for the farming community.
 
• It is celebrated **three times a year:** during **Chaitra Navratri** (spring), **Shravana** (monsoon), and **Ashwin Navratri** (autumn). However, the Shravan Harela is the most prominent.
 
• People sow seeds of **five or seven types of grains** in small baskets filled with soil ten days before Harela. On the festival day, these are harvested and worn on their heads as a symbol of prosperity.
 
• The festival is associated with **Hindu mythology**, celebrating the wedding of Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, both of whom are highly revered in Uttarakhand.
 
• Harela also serves as a reminder of the close connection between **humans and nature** and promotes environmental conservation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Significance of Harela Festival:**

 
 
• Harela celebrates the **agricultural heritage** of the hill state of Uttarakhand, emphasizing the importance of farming and the monsoon season for the local economy.
 
• The festival is also an occasion to promote **tree plantation**. On this day, people plant saplings as a gesture to preserve and protect the environment.
 
• In some regions, effigies of deities like Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati, made from leaves and grass, are worshipped as part of the Harela celebration.
 
 
 
• **Historical and Cultural Context:**
 
 
• Harela has been celebrated for centuries and holds **cultural significance** for the Kumaoni and Garhwali communities in Uttarakhand.
 
• The festival fosters a sense of **community bonding**, as families and neighbors come together to celebrate, sow seeds, and share traditional meals.
 
 
 
• **Other Festivals of Uttarakhand:**
 
 
• **Phool Dei:** A spring festival celebrating the arrival of the blossoming season.
 
• **Ghee Sankranti:** Also known as Olgia, it is a harvest festival where people express gratitude for agricultural abundance.
 
• **Basant Panchami:** Celebrated as the festival of kites and the worship of Goddess Saraswati.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Environmental Awareness:**

 
 
• Harela festival promotes **ecological balance** and environmental conservation, encouraging sustainable agricultural practices and tree plantation.
 
• It has become a platform for environmental awareness campaigns in modern times, with schools and organizations participating actively.
 
 
 
• **Revival of Traditions:**
 
 
• Efforts have been made by the Uttarakhand government and local communities to **revive and promote** the cultural significance of Harela.
 
• The festival is increasingly being recognized as a symbol of **sustainable development** and green initiatives in the region.

questions.question: Which of the following banks was merged with Indian Bank with effect from 1 April 2020?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Allahabad Bank**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Allahabad Bank**, one of the oldest banks in India, was merged with **Indian Bank** effective from **1 April 2020**. This decision was part of the Indian Government’s initiative to consolidate public sector banks for improved efficiency and financial stability.
 
• This merger aimed to create a stronger banking entity that would support economic growth and handle challenges like rising Non-Performing Assets (**NPA**) and increasing competition in the banking sector.
 
• The merger of **Allahabad Bank** with **Indian Bank** enabled operational synergies, better utilization of resources, and a more extensive customer base. *Hence, the correct answer is Allahabad Bank.*
 
• This consolidation process was part of the government’s larger reform strategy for public sector banks under the **Banking Sector Reform** announced by the Ministry of Finance in **2019**.
 
• Allahabad Bank ceased to exist as an independent entity after the merger and became part of the larger organizational structure of Indian Bank. *Hence, this merger was significant for the Indian banking industry.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Allahabad Bank:**

 
 
• **Allahabad Bank** was established in **1865** and was headquartered in **Kolkata**. It was one of the oldest joint stock banks in India.
 
• Before the merger, the bank provided various financial services, including deposits, loans, and banking products for individuals and businesses across India.
 
 
 
• **Indian Bank:**
 
 
• **Indian Bank** was established in **1907** and is headquartered in **Chennai**. It operates as a public sector bank under the ownership of the Government of India.
 
• Post-merger, Indian Bank became one of the largest public sector banks in India, offering comprehensive banking services to a wider customer base.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiative:**
 
 
• The merger was part of the **Banking Sector Reform 2019**, initiated by the Government of India, which aimed to consolidate public sector banks into fewer, larger entities.
 
• The reform targeted reducing operational inefficiencies, increasing competitiveness, and improving the overall health of the banking sector.
 
• The merger resulted in the creation of **12 strong and efficient public sector banks** from the existing 27 banks.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of Merger:**

 
 
• The merger created a larger banking entity with a wider geographical reach, improved financial stability, and increased operational efficiency.
 
• It helped in optimizing staff and resources while reducing overhead costs.
 
• The consolidated bank was able to leverage its size to offer competitive products and services, enhancing customer satisfaction.
 
 
 
• **Challenges:**
 
 
• The merger presented challenges such as cultural integration, harmonization of technology platforms, and addressing employee concerns.
 
• However, these challenges were systematically addressed to ensure a smooth transition and operational success.

questions.question: Ashadhi Bij, or the ______, is a distinguished cultural festival wherein the arrival of rain is celebrated.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kutchi New Year**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ashadhi Bij** is celebrated as the **Kutchi New Year**. It marks the beginning of the New Year for the Kutchi community in the western Indian state of Gujarat.
 
• The festival is celebrated on the **second day of the Shukla Paksha (waxing phase of the moon) of the Ashadha month**, as per the Hindu calendar.
 
• Ashadhi Bij is significant for the **Kutchi community**, as it symbolizes the arrival of the **monsoon season**. Farmers eagerly look forward to this day to assess the condition of the monsoon rains, which are crucial for agriculture. *Hence, the statement is correct.*
 
• The festival is celebrated with great enthusiasm, and people pray for good rains and prosperity. The community performs rituals and seeks blessings for a fruitful year ahead.
 
• The arrival of rains during Ashadhi Bij is a moment of joy and celebration, especially in the arid regions of Gujarat, where water is scarce. People show gratitude to nature for the rains. *Hence, the statement is correct.*
 
• The festival is also characterized by cultural events, traditional food, and community gatherings, which strengthen social bonds and preserve the rich heritage of the Kutchi community.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Kutchi New Year.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Significance of Ashadhi Bij:**

 
 
• **Monsoon Prediction:** Ashadhi Bij plays a critical role in forecasting the monsoon season. Farmers and local communities observe the atmosphere and wind patterns to predict rainfall during this festival.
 
• **Traditional Practices:** People engage in prayers and rituals, seeking blessings for a prosperous and rain-abundant year.
 
 
 
• **Kutchi Community:**
 
 
• The Kutchi community primarily resides in the **Kutch region** of Gujarat, India. This region is known for its unique cultural heritage, handicrafts, and arid climate.
 
• The celebration of Ashadhi Bij reflects the community's **deep connection to nature** and their dependence on rain for agricultural activities.
 
 
 
• **Other New Year Celebrations in India:**
 
 
• **Andhra New Year:** Celebrated as **Ugadi**, it marks the beginning of the Telugu calendar in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
 
• **Tamil New Year:** Known as **Puthandu**, it is celebrated on the first day of the Tamil month Chithirai.
 
• **Gond New Year:** Celebrated by the **Gond tribal community**, it highlights their cultural traditions and connection to nature.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Geographical and Cultural Context:**

 
 
• The **Kutch region**, located in Gujarat, is a **semi-arid area** where rainfall is essential for agriculture and survival. Festivals like Ashadhi Bij are important for assessing the monsoon and celebrating its arrival.
 
• **Cultural Significance:** Such festivals highlight the importance of traditional practices and rituals in preserving the community's identity and heritage.
 
 
 
• **Other Observations:**
 
 
• Ashadhi Bij is an example of how **regional festivals** reflect the socio-environmental realities of the area.
 
• It also emphasizes the importance of **sustainable living** and harmony with nature, which are integral to the Kutchi way of life.

questions.question: Which of the following awards is given by the K K Birla Foundation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vyas Samman**__.

__
 
• **The Vyas Samman** is a prestigious literary award presented annually by the **K K Birla Foundation**.
 
• It was established in **1991** and is awarded to an outstanding literary work in **Hindi** authored by an Indian citizen.
 
• The award recognizes a published work of fiction, poetry, drama, or criticism that has been released in the past **ten years**. *Hence, the correct answer is Vyas Samman.*
 
• The recipient of the Vyas Samman is awarded a cash prize of **INR 4 lakhs**, along with a citation and a plaque.
 
• This award is considered one of the most prestigious honors for contributions to Hindi literature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **K K Birla Foundation:**

 
 
• The **K K Birla Foundation**, established in **1991**, is known for promoting Indian literature, art, and education.
 
• Apart from the Vyas Samman, the foundation presents other awards, including the **Saraswati Samman**, **Shankar Puraskar**, and **Bihari Puraskar**.
 
 
 
• **Other Literary Awards by K K Birla Foundation:**
 
 
• **Saraswati Samman:** Recognizes exceptional literary works in any Indian language mentioned in the **Eighth Schedule** of the Indian Constitution. It carries a cash prize of **INR 15 lakhs**.
 
• **Bihari Puraskar:** Awarded for literary works in Hindi or Rajasthani by authors from Rajasthan.
 
• **Shankar Puraskar:** Presented for outstanding contributions to Indian philosophy and culture.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Awards:**
 
 
• **Sahitya Akademi Award:** This is awarded annually by the **Sahitya Akademi**, an autonomous organization under the Ministry of Culture, for literary works in **24 Indian languages**.
 
• **Jnanpith Award:** It is India’s highest literary honor, presented annually to authors for their contributions to Indian literature in **any recognized Indian language**.
 
• **Bharat Ratna:** India’s highest civilian award, awarded for exceptional service in fields like art, literature, science, and public service. It is not specific to literature.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Eligibility Criteria for Vyas Samman:**

 
 
• The award is granted to **Indian citizens** who have authored literary works in **Hindi.**
 
• Works must have been published in the past **10 years** to qualify for consideration.
 
 
 
• **Purpose of Literary Awards:**
 
 
• Literary awards like the Vyas Samman aim to **promote and recognize** exceptional contributions to Indian literature.
 
• They encourage authors to continue creating works that enrich the literary heritage of India.

questions.question: Which of the following battles was fought in 16th Century CE?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **First Battle of Panipat** was fought on **April 21, 1526**, marking it as a significant event in the **16th century CE**.
 
• This battle was fought between the forces of **Babur**, the founder of the Mughal Empire, and **Ibrahim Lodi**, the Sultan of Delhi.
 
• It marked the beginning of the **Mughal Empire in India** and ended the rule of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• Babur employed superior military tactics, including the use of **artillery**, which played a crucial role in his victory.
 
• The battle was significant as it introduced **gunpowder warfare** in the Indian subcontinent on a large scale.
 
• This victory paved the way for the establishment of a centralized Mughal administration in India.

__
 
• **First Battle of Panipat (1526):**

 
 
• This battle took place near the town of **Panipat**, located in present-day Haryana, India.
 
• The use of **tulughma (flanking tactics)** and artillery by Babur was instrumental in defeating Ibrahim Lodi's larger army.
 
• The victory established Babur as the ruler of Delhi and laid the foundation for the **Mughal Empire** in India.

• **Babur's Legacy:**
 
 
• Babur's victory at Panipat brought **new military techniques** to India, influencing subsequent warfare.
 
• He documented his campaigns and administration in his autobiography, **Baburnama**, which provides valuable insights into that era.

questions.question: Which of the following trenches is located in the Indian Ocean?

__
 
• **Sunda Trench** is located in the **Indian Ocean**, near the region of **Sumatra** and the **Java Islands**.
 
• It is one of the **deep-sea trenches** formed due to the subduction of the **Indo-Australian Plate beneath the Eurasian Plate**.
 
• The trench has a depth of approximately **7,725 meters** and is considered a critical area for studying plate tectonics and seismic activity. *Hence, Sunda Trench is the correct answer.*
 
• The other options provided in the question, such as the **Aleutian Trench**, **Ramapo Trench**, and **Atacama Trench**, are located in different oceans or regions and are not associated with the Indian Ocean.
 
• **Aleutian Trench** is found in the **North Pacific Ocean**, **Ramapo Trench** does not exist as a recognized geological feature, and **Atacama Trench** is located in the **Southeast Pacific Ocean** off the coast of Chile and Peru.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Sunda Trench:**

 
 
• Located in the **northeastern Indian Ocean**, the Sunda Trench plays a significant role in the region's tectonic activity.
 
• The trench is formed due to the **subduction of the Indo-Australian Plate** under the **Eurasian Plate**, leading to frequent **earthquakes** and volcanic activities.
 
• One of the most notable seismic events associated with this trench was the **2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami**, which caused widespread devastation.
 
 
 
• **Other Trenches in Context:**
 
 
• **Aleutian Trench:** Located in the **North Pacific Ocean**, it is associated with the subduction of the Pacific Plate beneath the North American Plate.
 
• **Atacama Trench:** Found in the **Southeast Pacific Ocean**, it is formed due to the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate.
 
• **Ramapo Trench:** Not recognized as a geological feature, it seems to be erroneously mentioned in the question.

• **Depth and Significance:** The Sunda Trench has a depth of **7,725 meters**, making it one of the deeper trenches in the Indian Ocean. It is a hotspot for studying **subduction zones** and the **geodynamics** of the region.
 
• **Seismic Activity:** Earthquakes originating from this trench have caused major tsunamis, such as the **2004 Indian Ocean tsunami**, which had a magnitude of **9.1–9.3**.
 
• **Plate Tectonics:** The trench is a key example of **oceanic plate subduction**, offering insights into the interactions between the **Indo-Australian Plate** and the **Eurasian Plate**.

__
 
• **The Rampurva bull capital** was discovered at the archaeological site of Rampurva in the state of **Bihar**.
 
• This capital is one of the **Ashokan pillars**, which were commissioned by Emperor **Ashoka** during the Maurya dynasty in the 3rd century BCE.
 
• The Rampurva bull capital is noted for its exquisite **sculptural craftsmanship** and is considered a masterpiece of Mauryan art.
 
• The bull capital from Rampurva is now displayed in the **Rashtrapati Bhavan**, the official residence of the **President of India**, located in **New Delhi**.

• The pillars of Ashoka are a series of columns distributed across the Indian subcontinent. They were erected by **Emperor Ashoka** during his reign from **268 to 232 BCE**.
 
• Each pillar is made of a single piece of **polished sandstone**, and most are topped with animal capitals such as lions, bulls, and elephants.
 
• The pillars bear inscriptions in the **Brahmi script**, promoting Ashoka's policies of **Dhamma** (righteousness) and his messages of peace and non-violence.
 
 
 
• **Location of other Ashokan Pillars:**
 
 
• Apart from Rampurva, other famous Ashokan pillars include those at **Sarnath**, **Lauriya Nandangarh**, and **Vaishali**.
 
• The **Sarnath lion capital**, which is now the **National Emblem of India**, is an iconic representation of Ashoka's reign.

• It houses a **museum** that displays various artifacts, including the Rampurva bull capital, reflecting India's historical and cultural legacy.

• **Discovery of the Rampurva Bull Capital:**

 
 
• The Rampurva bull capital was discovered during archaeological excavations in **Rampurva, West Champaran district, Bihar**.
 
• It is one of the few surviving examples of Mauryan art and architecture, reflecting the technical and artistic excellence of the period.
 
 
 
• **Symbolism of the Bull:**
 
 
• The bull is associated with **agriculture** and **prosperity** in Indian culture and is a recurring motif in Ashokan pillars.
 
• It also symbolizes **power**, **strength**, and **endurance**, qualities that were significant to the Mauryan empire.

• It is renowned for its vibrant festivals like **Raas Leela** and **Ali Ai Ligang**, which reflect the rich cultural traditions of the region.

questions.question: Which of the following metals does NOT belong to the top of the activity series?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lead**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Activity Series of Metals:** The activity series of metals is a list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity, starting from the most reactive to the least reactive. Highly reactive metals include **Sodium**, **Magnesium**, and **Aluminium**, which are at the top of the series.
 
• Metals at the top of the activity series can easily lose electrons and participate in chemical reactions, making them highly reactive.
 
• **Lead:** Lead is placed lower in the activity series because it is less reactive compared to metals like Sodium, Magnesium, and Aluminium. It does not belong to the top of the activity series. *Hence, Lead is the correct option.*
 
• **Sodium:** Sodium is a highly reactive alkali metal and is placed at the top of the activity series. It reacts vigorously with water and oxygen. *Hence, Sodium is incorrect.*
 
• **Magnesium:** Magnesium is also highly reactive and part of the top activity series. It reacts with acids and oxygen to form compounds. *Hence, Magnesium is incorrect.*
 
• **Aluminium:** Aluminium is a reactive metal commonly placed high in the activity series. It forms a protective oxide layer, making it suitable for various applications. *Hence, Aluminium is incorrect.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Lead.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Activity Series of Metals:**

 
 
• The activity series is a scientific arrangement of metals based on their ability to displace hydrogen from acids or water. Metals at the top are highly reactive, while metals near the bottom are less reactive.
 
• Highly reactive metals like **Sodium** and **Potassium** react vigorously with water and even air. Moderately reactive metals like Zinc and Iron react with acids but not with cold water.
 
• Metals lower in the series, such as **Lead**, **Copper**, and **Gold**, are less reactive and do not readily form compounds.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Each Metal:**
 
 
• **Sodium:** Sodium is a soft, highly reactive metal used in the production of chemicals, soaps, and batteries. It reacts explosively with water.
 
• **Magnesium:** Magnesium is a lightweight metal used in alloys, fireworks, and medicines. It burns with a bright white flame.
 
• **Aluminium:** Aluminium is widely used in construction, packaging, and aerospace due to its strength, lightweight nature, and corrosion resistance.
 
• **Lead:** Lead is a dense, less reactive metal used in batteries, radiation shielding, and ammunition. Its low reactivity makes it suitable for applications requiring stability.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Activity Series:**
 
 
• The activity series helps predict the outcomes of chemical reactions, such as displacement reactions and metal extraction from ores.
 
• It also aids in understanding corrosion resistance, where less reactive metals are preferred for long-term use.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Observations on Reactivity:**

 
 
• Highly reactive metals like **Sodium** and **Potassium** are stored under oil to prevent reactions with air or moisture.
 
• Less reactive metals like **Lead** and **Gold** are used in applications requiring stability and resistance to corrosion.
 
 
 
• **Displacement Reactions:**
 
 
• Metals higher in the activity series can displace metals lower in the series in chemical reactions. For example, Zinc can displace Lead from its compounds.
 
• The activity series is vital in metallurgy, guiding the extraction and refining of metals from ores.

questions.question: The Constitution of India as adopted on 26 November 1949 contained a Preamble, 395 Articles and ______ Schedules. 7

__
 
• The **Constitution of India** was adopted on **26 November 1949**, and it came into effect on **26 January 1950**.
 
• At the time of its adoption, the Constitution consisted of a **Preamble**, **395 Articles**, and **8 Schedules**. *Hence, the correct answer is 8.*
 
• The **Schedules** in the Constitution are lists or tables that categorize and tabulate bureaucratic activity and policy of the Government of India. These schedules provide additional details or clarify certain provisions of the Constitution.
 
• The **8 Schedules** initially included provisions like the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha, administration and control of scheduled areas, languages, and other administrative details.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is 8.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Schedules of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• Initially, there were only **8 Schedules** in the Constitution, but over time, the number of schedules has increased to **12** through various amendments.
 
• The additional schedules were added to accommodate the evolving needs of the Indian polity and administration. For example, the **9th Schedule** was added by the **First Amendment Act, 1951**, and the **10th Schedule** was added by the **52nd Amendment Act, 1985**.
 
 
 
• **Details of the Original 8 Schedules:**
 
 
• **First Schedule:** Lists the names of states and union territories and their territorial jurisdiction.
 
• **Second Schedule:** Specifies the emoluments, allowances, and privileges of the President, Governors, Judges, and other constitutional authorities.
 
• **Third Schedule:** Contains the forms of oaths or affirmations to be made by constitutional office holders.
 
• **Fourth Schedule:** Allocates seats for each state and union territory in the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
 
• **Fifth Schedule:** Deals with the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
 
• **Sixth Schedule:** Contains provisions for the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
 
• **Seventh Schedule:** Specifies the distribution of powers and functions between the Union and the States through three lists – Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.
 
• **Eighth Schedule:** Lists the official languages recognized by the Constitution. Initially, it included **14 languages**, which has now increased to **22 languages** through amendments.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Constitution of India** is the longest written constitution in the world, containing 395 Articles divided into 22 Parts and 8 Schedules at the time of its adoption.
 
• Over the years, the Constitution has undergone over **100 amendments**, which have added more Articles, Parts, and Schedules.
 
• The **Schedules** are critical to understanding the administrative and legislative framework of the Indian government. They provide clarity and structure to the provisions of the Constitution.
 
• The Constitution has evolved to address the changing socio-political, economic, and cultural needs of the nation while adhering to its core principles of democracy, secularism, and federalism.

• The **Congress Party** in **1976** established the **Sardar Swaran Singh Committee** to provide recommendations on incorporating **Fundamental Duties** into the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• This step was taken during the time of the **Emergency**, declared by the then Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**, as an effort to strengthen national discipline and responsibility among citizens.
 
• The committee, chaired by **Sardar Swaran Singh**, proposed the incorporation of Fundamental Duties as a part of the Constitution to promote a sense of duty and patriotism. *Hence, the committee's name in the question is correct.*
 
• Based on the recommendations of the **Sardar Swaran Singh Committee**, the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976** added **Part IVA** and **Article 51A** to the Constitution, which enlists the Fundamental Duties of citizens.
 
• The original list contained **10 Fundamental Duties**, which were later increased to **11** by the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act in 2002**. This demonstrates the enduring influence of the committee's recommendations.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is Sardar Swaran Singh.*

• **Sardar Swaran Singh Committee:**

• The committee suggested that citizens should have certain responsibilities towards the nation to complement the Fundamental Rights already present in the Constitution.
 
• It is noteworthy that the committee’s recommendations were part of a broader effort to enhance national integrity and discipline during the period of Emergency (1975–77).
 
 
 
• **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976):**
 
 
• This amendment is often referred to as the **“Mini Constitution”** because of its wide-ranging changes.
 
• It added **Part IVA** to the Constitution, which includes **Article 51A**, listing the Fundamental Duties.
 
• The amendment also made significant changes to the Preamble, Directive Principles of State Policy, and strengthened the central government’s powers.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Duties:**
 
 
• The Fundamental Duties are inspired by the **USSR Constitution** and are meant to emphasize the moral obligations of citizens.
 
• Examples of Fundamental Duties include respecting the Constitution, cherishing the noble ideals of the freedom struggle, and protecting the sovereignty and unity of India.
 
• The 11th Fundamental Duty, added by the **86th Amendment**, emphasizes the duty of parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Characteristics of Fundamental Duties:**

questions.question: Which of the following was one of the capitals of the Vijayanagara empire?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chandragiri**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chandragiri** was one of the capitals of the **Vijayanagara Empire**, especially during its later stages. The empire is known for its rich cultural and architectural heritage.
 
• The **Vijayanagara Empire**, founded in 1336 by the Sangama dynasty, initially had its capital at Hampi (also called Vijayanagara). However, in the later years, especially during the rule of the Aravidu dynasty, the capital was shifted to Chandragiri.
 
• Chandragiri is located in present-day **Andhra Pradesh**, near Tirupati, and was strategically important due to its geographic location and natural fortifications.
 
• The fort at Chandragiri is a significant architectural marvel, showcasing the influence of **South Indian temple architecture** and military design. It stands as a testament to the ingenuity of the Vijayanagara rulers.
 
• The shift of the capital to Chandragiri occurred after the decline of the Vijayanagara Empire's power, largely due to invasions by the Deccan Sultanates after the Battle of Talikota in 1565.
 
• Chandragiri remained an important administrative center for the Aravidu dynasty, which was the last ruling dynasty of the Vijayanagara Empire, until their decline in the 17th century.
 
• The other options mentioned in the question—**Chunar, Chausa, and Champaner**—were not associated with the Vijayanagara Empire. They were historically significant in other regions of India but not related to the empire's capitals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chandragiri:**

 
 
• Located near **Tirupati** in Andhra Pradesh, Chandragiri is known for its majestic fort, which is an excellent example of South Indian architecture.
 
• The fort is believed to have been built in the 11th century by the Yadava rulers and was later captured by the rulers of Vijayanagara in the 14th century.
 
• Chandragiri gained prominence as the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire under the Aravidu dynasty, after the fall of Hampi.
 
 
 
• **Vijayanagara Empire:**
 
 
• The Vijayanagara Empire was established in 1336 by **Harihara I and Bukka Raya I** of the Sangama dynasty.
 
• It was renowned for its contributions to **art, culture, architecture, and administration**. Hampi, its original capital, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site today.
 
• The empire played a significant role in resisting the expansion of Islamic sultanates in South India and preserving Hindu culture.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Chunar:** Located in Uttar Pradesh, Chunar is known for its fort, which was significant during the Mughal and British periods, but it had no connection to the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• **Chausa:** A historical location in Bihar, Chausa is famous for the Battle of Chausa in 1539, where Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun. It is unrelated to the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• **Champaner:** Situated in Gujarat, Champaner was the capital of the Gujarat Sultanate and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was not associated with the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Battle of Talikota:**

 
 
• The Battle of Talikota (1565) was a significant event that marked the beginning of the end for the Vijayanagara Empire. It was fought between the Vijayanagara Empire and the combined armies of the Deccan Sultanates.
 
• The defeat of Vijayanagara led to the sacking of Hampi, and the empire's capital was subsequently moved to Chandragiri.
 
 
 
• **Architectural Significance:**
 
 
• The Vijayanagara rulers were great patrons of art and architecture. Chandragiri fort and other structures built during their reign exhibit intricate carvings and Dravidian architectural styles.
 
• The empire also contributed significantly to South Indian temple architecture, with notable examples like the Virupaksha Temple and Vittala Temple in Hampi.

questions.question: According to the special theory of relativity which of the following is NOT relative?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Velocity of light**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **special theory of relativity**, formulated by Albert Einstein in **1905**, revolutionized the understanding of space, time, and motion. It introduced the concept that many quantities previously considered absolute are actually relative.
 
• Among the quantities listed in the question:
 
 
• **Time interval between two events:** In relativity, time is not absolute. Observers in different inertial frames may measure different time intervals for the same pair of events. This is known as **time dilation**. Hence, this quantity is relative.
 
• **Simultaneity:** Events that appear simultaneous to one observer may not be simultaneous to another observer moving at a different velocity. This concept is a direct consequence of relativity, making simultaneity a relative concept.
 
• **Length of an object:** According to relativity, the length of an object can change depending on the relative motion between the observer and the object. This phenomenon is termed as **length contraction**. Thus, length is also relative.
 
• **Velocity of light:** Unlike the other quantities, the velocity of light in a vacuum is an **absolute constant**, independent of the motion of the source or the observer. This was confirmed by the famous **Michelson-Morley experiment**, which demonstrated that the speed of light is always approximately **299,792 kilometers per second**. Hence, this quantity is NOT relative.
 
 
 
• Therefore, the correct answer is **Velocity of light**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Special Theory of Relativity:**

 
 
• Proposed by **Albert Einstein** in **1905**, it is based on two postulates:

 
 
• The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference.
 
• The speed of light in vacuum is constant and does not depend on the motion of the source or the observer.
 
 
 
• It challenged classical mechanics and introduced concepts such as **time dilation**, **length contraction**, and the equivalence of mass and energy (**E=mc²**).
 
 
 
• **Michelson-Morley Experiment:**
 
 
• Conducted by **Albert A. Michelson** and **Edward W. Morley** in **1887**, this experiment aimed to detect the relative motion of matter through the hypothetical "ether."
 
• It proved that the speed of light is constant in all directions, which laid the foundation for Einstein’s theory of relativity.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Relativity:**
 
 
• Relativity has profound implications in **modern physics**, influencing areas like **astrophysics**, **GPS technology**, and **particle physics**.
 
• For example, **GPS satellites** account for relativistic effects to provide accurate location data.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The velocity of light is a universal constant and is denoted by **c**.
 
• Its value is approximately **3 x 10⁸ m/s**, and it is essential for calculations in electromagnetic theory and relativity.
 
• The invariance of the speed of light is a cornerstone of the **special theory of relativity**, distinguishing it from classical Newtonian physics.
 
• Relativity has been experimentally verified through phenomena such as **muon decay**, observations in particle accelerators, and **cosmic ray interactions**.

questions.question: Which of the following land revenue systems is also known as ‘Munro System’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ryotwari**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ryotwari System** is also referred to as the **'Munro System.'**
 
• This land revenue system was introduced by the British in areas like **Madras, Bombay, and Assam.**
 
• Under the Ryotwari system, the revenue was collected directly from the **cultivators (Ryots)** by the government, eliminating the role of intermediaries such as zamindars.
 
• It was pioneered by **Thomas Munro**, a British administrator and later Governor of Madras, hence named after him.
 
• The system ensured that the cultivators were recognized as the owners of the land and were liable to pay the revenue directly to the state.
 
• The revenue was assessed based on the type of soil, crops grown, and productivity of the land. **Periodic surveys** were conducted to update assessments.
 
• It was deemed beneficial for the cultivators compared to Zamindari and Mahalwari systems, which involved intermediaries and often led to exploitation.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is Ryotwari.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Zamindari System:**

 
 
• Under this system, the revenue was collected by **Zamindars**, who acted as intermediaries between the government and the cultivators.
 
• Introduced by the British in **Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, and parts of northern India**, it often led to exploitation of cultivators due to high revenue demands.
 
 
 
• **Mahalwari System:**
 
 
• Introduced in **northwest India** (including Punjab, parts of UP, and Delhi), this system involved revenue collection from a village or group of villages (Mahal).
 
• The revenue was shared among all cultivators of the Mahal, often leading to collective responsibility for payments.
 
 
 
• **Ijaradari System:**
 
 
• This was a form of revenue farming where the rights to collect revenue were auctioned to the highest bidder, known as the **Ijaradar**.
 
• It was prevalent in certain regions during the early British rule but fell out of favor due to inefficiencies and exploitation.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Ryotwari System:**
 
 
• Cultivators were acknowledged as **landowners.**
 
• Revenue assessment was based on **soil quality, productivity, and type of crops grown.**
 
• Periodic **revenue surveys** were conducted to ensure fair assessment.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:**

 
 
• The Ryotwari system was introduced during the **early 19th century**, primarily in regions where Zamindari failed to work effectively.
 
• Thomas Munro played a key role in its introduction in the **Madras Presidency**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with other systems:**
 
 
• Unlike Zamindari and Mahalwari systems, Ryotwari ensured **direct interaction between the cultivators and the government.**
 
• This reduced exploitation and improved accountability in revenue collection.

questions.question: Cinnabar when heated in air gets converted into oxide of ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**mercury**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cinnabar (HgS)** is a naturally occurring mineral of **mercury sulfide**, and it is the primary ore used for the extraction of mercury.
 
• When **cinnabar (HgS) is heated in air,** it undergoes a chemical reaction to form **mercury(II) oxide (HgO)**. This is an oxidation process because cinnabar reacts with oxygen present in the air.
 
• The reaction can be represented as: HgS + O₂ → HgO + SO₂. This shows that cinnabar is converted into mercury oxide and sulfur dioxide gas is released as a by-product.
 
• Further heating of mercury oxide (HgO) leads to its decomposition into **elemental mercury (Hg)** and oxygen gas (O₂). This step is typically carried out to extract pure mercury.
 
• Hence, when cinnabar is heated in air, it gets converted into an **oxide of mercury**, confirming that the correct answer is **mercury**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Cinnabar (HgS):**

 
 
• Cinnabar is the most important ore of mercury. It has a bright red or reddish-brown color and has been used historically as a pigment in art and decoration.
 
• It is composed of mercury sulfide (HgS) and has a high mercury content, which makes it a valuable source for the extraction of mercury.
 
 
 
• **Properties of Mercury:**
 
 
• **Mercury** is a liquid metal at room temperature and is known for its high density and unique property of forming amalgams with other metals.
 
• Mercury has applications in thermometers, barometers, fluorescent lamps, and dental amalgams. However, its use is being reduced due to its toxic effects.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Reactions Involved:**
 
 
• **Oxidation of Cinnabar:** When cinnabar reacts with oxygen, it forms mercury oxide (HgO) and sulfur dioxide gas (SO₂).
 
• **Decomposition of Mercury Oxide:** Further heating of mercury oxide results in its decomposition into elemental mercury and oxygen gas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Alternative Uses of Cinnabar:**

 
 
• Apart from being a source of mercury, cinnabar has also been used as a pigment called vermilion for centuries.
 
• Due to its high toxicity, modern uses of cinnabar are limited, and handling requires proper safety measures.
 
 
 
• **Health and Environmental Concerns:**
 
 
• Mercury and its compounds, including cinnabar, are highly toxic. Prolonged exposure can lead to severe health issues, including neurological damage.
 
• Environmental pollution due to mercury is a major concern, as it can accumulate in the food chain, particularly in aquatic ecosystems.

• The book won the **Man Booker Prize** in **2002**, cementing Yann Martel's position as a prominent contemporary writer.
 
• Yann Martel was born in **Salamanca, Spain**, in **1963**, but he is a Canadian writer. His works are known for their philosophical themes and exploration of complex human emotions.

questions.question: Which of the following is the northernmost forest zone and forms a circumpolar belt of more or less closed forests growing in harsh climates between the latitudes 50°N to 70°N?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Boreal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Boreal forests** are also referred to as the **Taiga**. They represent the world's largest terrestrial biome, forming a circumpolar belt around the **northern hemisphere**.
 
• These forests are located between the latitudes of **50ºN to 70ºN**, spanning countries like **Canada, Russia, Sweden, Finland, Norway, and Alaska**.
 
• The climate in the boreal forest zone is **harsh**, characterized by **long, cold winters** and **short summers**. The region experiences **low precipitation**, mainly in the form of snow. *Hence, this is the correct answer.*
 
• The vegetation in boreal forests is dominated by **coniferous trees** such as spruce, pine, fir, and larch. These trees are well-adapted to the cold climate and poor soil conditions.
 
• Boreal forests are an essential carbon sink, absorbing significant amounts of **carbon dioxide** from the atmosphere and contributing to the regulation of the global climate. *Hence, Boreal forests play a vital ecological role.*
 
• The fauna in boreal forests includes species adapted to cold climates, such as **bears, wolves, moose, lynxes, and birds** like owls and woodpeckers.
 
• Economic activities in the boreal region are generally limited to **logging, mining, and hunting**, as the climatic conditions make agriculture challenging. *Hence, boreal forests have limited human activities.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Boreal.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Global Forest Zones:**

 
 
• **Tropical forests:** Found near the equator, these forests experience warm and humid climates. Examples include the **Amazon Rainforest** and the Congo Basin.
 
• **Torrid forests:** This term is less commonly used and often overlaps with tropical regions. It refers to forests in regions with extreme heat and high rainfall.
 
• **Temperate forests:** Found in regions with moderate climates, such as Europe, North America, and parts of Asia. These forests have a mix of **deciduous** and **coniferous trees**.
 
• **Boreal forests:** These forests form a circumpolar belt in the northern hemisphere and are characterized by cold climates and coniferous vegetation.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Boreal Forests:**
 
 
• **Soil:** Boreal forests have **thin, acidic, and nutrient-poor soil** due to slow decomposition rates.
 
• **Climate:** The region experiences **subarctic climates** with temperatures ranging from **-50°C to 30°C**.
 
• **Importance:** Boreal forests are crucial for **biodiversity** conservation and **carbon sequestration**, acting as a buffer against climate change.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Threats to Boreal Forests:**

 
 
• **Deforestation:** Logging and mining activities pose significant threats to boreal forests.
 
• **Climate change:** Rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns are impacting the ecological balance of boreal regions.
 
• **Wildfires:** Increased frequency of wildfires due to dry conditions and global warming is a growing concern.
 
 
 
• **Conservation Efforts:**
 
 
• Countries like **Canada** and **Russia** have implemented policies to protect boreal forests through **national parks** and conservation programs.
 
• **International organizations** such as the UN are promoting sustainable practices to conserve these forests.

questions.question: The term 'Arribada' is associated with which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Olive Ridley turtle**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **‘Arribada’** refers to a unique phenomenon where thousands of **Olive Ridley turtles** come together on specific beaches for mass nesting. This event is a synchronized and remarkable natural occurrence.
 
• During the **Arribada**, female turtles come ashore to lay eggs, often at night, in large groups. This ensures the survival of a significant number of hatchlings despite predators.
 
• The term **‘Arribada’** is derived from the Spanish word meaning ‘arrival.’ This phenomenon is most commonly observed along the coasts of **India, Costa Rica, and Mexico**.
 
• In **India**, the Gahirmatha Beach in Odisha and the Rushikulya River mouth are globally recognized as important nesting sites for the **Olive Ridley turtles**.
 
• This synchronized nesting enhances the chances of survival as it overwhelms predators, ensuring that a significant number of eggs and hatchlings survive. This strategy is termed **safety in numbers**.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is Olive Ridley turtle.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Olive Ridley Turtles:**

 
 
• The **Olive Ridley turtle** is one of the smallest species of sea turtles, named for its olive-colored shell.
 
• These turtles are classified as **vulnerable** by the **International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)** due to threats like habitat loss, fishing nets, and egg poaching.
 
• **Scientific Name:** Lepidochelys olivacea. They are found in warm and tropical waters, primarily in the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Ganges Dolphin:** The Ganges River dolphin is a freshwater species found in the Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers. It is unrelated to the term **‘Arribada’**.
 
• **Tiger:** Tigers are terrestrial predators and have no relation to the term **‘Arribada’**. They are typically solitary animals.
 
• **Crocodile:** Crocodiles are reptiles that inhabit freshwater and saltwater environments. They also do not exhibit mass nesting behavior like the Olive Ridley turtles.
 
 
 
• **Conservation Efforts:**
 
 
• Efforts to protect Olive Ridley turtles include creating **protected nesting sites** and implementing **fishing bans** during the nesting season.
 
• Programs like **Operation Kachhapa** in Odisha aim to conserve these turtles by reducing human-related threats.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mass Nesting Phenomenon:** Mass nesting events like the **Arribada** are rare and occur in only a few places globally, making their conservation critical for maintaining biodiversity.
 
• **Threats to Olive Ridley Turtles:** These include **poaching** of eggs, **accidental capture in fishing nets**, climate change affecting nesting sites, and pollution in the oceans.
 
• **Legal Protections:** In **India**, Olive Ridley turtles are protected under the **Wildlife Protection Act of 1972**, which prohibits hunting and trade of these turtles and their eggs.

questions.question: Which of the following states is NOT drained by the river Tapi?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajasthan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **river Tapi**, also called the **Tapti River**, originates from the **Satpura ranges** in Madhya Pradesh near Multai in Betul district.
 
• It flows through **Madhya Pradesh**, **Maharashtra**, and **Gujarat** before draining into the Arabian Sea. *Hence, these states are drained by the river Tapi.*
 
• The river does not flow through **Rajasthan**. Rajasthan lies to the northwest of the river’s path and is primarily drained by rivers like the Chambal, Luni, and Banas. *Hence, Rajasthan is NOT drained by the Tapi River.*
 
• The Tapi River is known for its importance in the irrigation and water supply of the regions it traverses, but Rajasthan does not benefit from it due to its geographical location.
 
• The states of Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Madhya Pradesh have significant parts of their territories influenced by the Tapi River, contributing to agriculture, water usage, and local ecosystems. *Hence, the correct answer is Rajasthan.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **River Tapi:**

 
 
• The **Tapi River** has a total length of approximately **724 km**. It is one of the major rivers of peninsular India.
 
• It originates from **Multai** in the Satpura ranges in **Madhya Pradesh** and flows westward, making it unique among rivers in India that flow towards the Arabian Sea.
 
• The river basin covers approximately **65,145 square kilometers**, spreading across Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat.
 
 
 
• **States Drained by Tapi:**
 
 
• **Madhya Pradesh:** The river originates here and flows through regions like Betul and Burhanpur.
 
• **Maharashtra:** The Tapi River flows through districts like Jalgaon and Dhule, contributing significantly to agriculture in the region.
 
• **Gujarat:** Tapi enters Gujarat near Surat and drains into the Arabian Sea. The city of Surat is located on the banks of the Tapi River.
 
 
 
• **Rivers in Rajasthan:**
 
 
• **Chambal River:** A major river of Rajasthan, it flows through the southeastern part of the state.
 
• **Luni River:** Known as the lifeline of western Rajasthan, it is a seasonal river that flows through arid regions.
 
• **Banas River:** A tributary of the Chambal, flowing through eastern Rajasthan.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Geographical Features:**

 
 
• The **Tapi River basin** is bordered by the Satpura hills in the north, the Ajanta ranges in the south, and the Arabian Sea in the west.
 
• The river is known for its westward flow, unlike many other rivers in India that flow eastward.
 
 
 
• **Economic Importance:**

questions.question: Who among the following summoned the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir?

__
 
• **Kanishka**, the famous ruler of the **Kushan dynasty**, convened the **Fourth Buddhist Council** in **Kashmir** around **78 CE**. This council is considered highly significant in the history of Buddhism.
 
• The council was held under the patronage of Kanishka, who was a great supporter of Buddhism. It aimed to resolve disputes and consolidate Buddhist teachings into a unified doctrine.
 
• It was during this council that the **Mahayana school of Buddhism** gained prominence, distinguishing itself from the earlier **Theravada** tradition.
 
• The council was presided over by renowned Buddhist scholars like **Vasumitra** and **Ashvaghosha**, who played crucial roles in compiling Buddhist texts and promoting the Mahayana philosophy.
 
• The **Fourth Buddhist Council** led to the **translation of Buddhist texts** into Sanskrit, marking a significant shift from the earlier use of Pali as the primary language for Buddhist scriptures.
 
• This council also helped in the establishment of Buddhism as a widespread religion beyond India, influencing regions like **Central Asia**, **China**, and **Southeast Asia**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kanishka:**

 
 
• Kanishka was the **most notable ruler** of the Kushan dynasty, ruling during the **1st and 2nd centuries CE**. He is renowned for his patronage of Buddhism and his efforts to spread the religion across his vast empire.
 
• His empire extended from **Central Asia** to parts of present-day India, encompassing regions like **Kashmir**, **Afghanistan**, and **northern India**.
 
• He introduced the **Kanishka era**, which began in **78 CE**, and is often linked to the development of the **Saka calendar**.
 
 
 
• **Other Buddhist Councils:**
 
 
• **First Buddhist Council:** Held at Rajagriha shortly after Buddha's death to compile his teachings.
 
• **Second Buddhist Council:** Convened at Vaishali to address disputes over monastic rules.
 
• **Third Buddhist Council:** Held in Pataliputra under the patronage of Emperor Ashoka to purify the Buddhist community.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Fourth Buddhist Council:**
 
 
• It marked the **division of Buddhism** into Mahayana and Theravada schools.
 
• The council paved the way for the spread of Buddhism to **China**, **Japan**, and other parts of Asia.
 
• It promoted the **scholarly compilation** and systematization of Buddhist texts, ensuring their preservation for future generations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Ashvaghosha:** A renowned poet and philosopher, he was a central figure in propagating Mahayana Buddhism and contributed to Buddhist literature.
 
• **Language Shift:** The decision to translate Buddhist scriptures into Sanskrit during the Fourth Buddhist Council helped in the global dissemination of Buddhism.
 
• **Impact on Art and Culture:** Kanishka’s reign saw the flourishing of the **Gandhara and Mathura schools of art**, which combined Indian and Hellenistic artistic styles.

questions.question: In India, angel tax is related to ______.

• **Angel tax** is a tax levied on the capital raised by unlisted companies (start-ups) through the issuance of shares, where the share price is seen to exceed the fair market value of the company.
 
• This tax is applicable under **Section 56(2)(vii)(b)** of the **Income Tax Act, 1961**. It is commonly referred to as the "angel tax" because it often impacts angel investors who fund start-ups.
 
• The tax is imposed on the amount that exceeds the fair market value of the shares issued by the start-up, and this excess amount is treated as income in the hands of the company. *Hence, start-ups are directly related to angel tax.*
 
• Angel tax was introduced in **2012** to prevent unaccounted money from being disguised as investments. It affects start-ups when they receive funding from domestic investors.
 
• The tax is only applicable to unlisted companies, and foreign investors are exempt from it. This ensures that it primarily impacts Indian investors funding Indian start-ups.
 
• The **Government of India**, through the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**, has provided exemptions to recognized start-ups from angel tax, subject to certain conditions.
 
• This exemption aims to foster innovation and reduce the compliance burden on start-ups, ensuring that they can focus on their growth without undue financial strain. *Hence, the correct answer is start-ups.*

__
 
• **Purpose of Angel Tax:**

 
 
• Angel tax was implemented to prevent money laundering and to ensure that investments in start-ups are genuine.
 
• It ensures that start-ups do not use inflated valuations to route black money into the financial system under the guise of investments.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Angel Tax:**
 
 
• Introduced in **2012** under the **Finance Act.**
 
• Applies to unlisted companies receiving capital from domestic investors exceeding the fair market value of shares.
 
• Foreign investors are exempted from angel tax.
 
 
 
• **Exemption for Start-ups:**
 
 
• Start-ups recognized by the **DPIIT** are exempt from angel tax, provided they meet specific criteria such as turnover limits and filing declarations.
 
• This step was taken to promote the start-up ecosystem in India, which is vital for economic growth and job creation.
 
 
 
• **Challenges Related to Angel Tax:**
 
 
• Start-ups often face scrutiny for valuations, which can delay funding and create compliance burdens.
 
• Despite exemptions, there are operational challenges, including proving the fair market value of shares.

• **Government Initiatives:**

 
 
• The **Startup India Initiative**, launched in **2016**, aims to promote innovation and entrepreneurship by providing tax exemptions, regulatory support, and funding opportunities.
 
• Recognized start-ups can avail of tax exemptions under Section **80-IAC** of the Income Tax Act for three consecutive years.
 
 
 
• **Other Related Terms:**
 
 
• **Venture Capital:** A form of private equity financing provided to start-ups and small businesses with high growth potential.
